title: How life and computation began
schrodinger: In What Is Life? (1944), Erwin Schrödinger framed the foundational puzzle: while closed physical systems decay toward disorder, open living systems stay ordered by continuously drawing free energy ('negative entropy') from gradients like warm alkaline vents.
bennett: In A Brief History of Intelligence (2023), Max Bennett treats early pre-neural chemistry as survival metabolism prior to minds—placing the start of brain intelligence 3.5 billion years later when animals first steer.
aguera: In What Is Life?: Evolution as Computation and What Is Intelligence? (2025)
column8: Blaise Agüera y Arcas argues life begins as computation itself: in his team's BFF Turing-tape experiments
column9: random programs bumping into each other with no fitness goal spontaneously form self-copying replicators.

title: The genetic code-script and the cell as constructor
schrodinger: Nine years before Watson and Crick (1953), Schrödinger deduced in What Is Life? that genes must be an 'aperiodic crystal'—a stable, non-repeating chain of molecular letters acting as a digital code-script against thermal noise.
bennett: Bennett notes that DNA evolution learns across generations by trial and error
aguera: but cannot rewrite behavior inside a single afternoon—setting up the later need for fast neural learning.
column8: Agüera y Arcas connects DNA and the ribosome directly to John von Neumann's 1940s proof of self-reproducing automata: DNA is the passive instruction tape, while the ribosome is the physical tape-reading constructor that builds another cell.

title: Symbiogenesis: when two replicators merge into one
schrodinger: Swallowing an oxygen-breathing bacterium (mitochondria) and later a cyanobacterium (chloroplast) multiplied usable free energy per gene roughly ten-thousand-fold, paying the thermodynamic price for huge complex-cell genomes.
bennett: Bennett focuses downstream of complex cells: once multicellular bodies exist and compete as predators and prey
aguera: natural selection is forced to wire fast sensors and nerves.
column8: Agüera y Arcas places symbiogenesis—championed by Lynn Margulis—at the very center of evolution. Rather than advancing only by 'red in tooth and claw' competition, major leaps happen when separate computational replicators fuse into a cooperative whole, from BFF tapes and mitochondria to multicellularity and human-AI teams.

title: Breakthrough 1: Steering through a 3D world
schrodinger: Fast electrical spikes along cell membranes trade a tiny metabolic ATP bill to carry signals thousands of times faster than random molecular diffusion.
bennett: Max Bennett names Early Cambrian bilaterian navigation Breakthrough 1 (Steering): clustering sensors at a front head and tagging stimuli with positive or negative valence ('approach food, avoid harm') creates the basic loop every vertebrate brain still rests on.
aguera: Agüera y Arcas traces animal steering back to bacterial run-and-tumble chemotaxis and Jakob von Uexküll's Umwelt: even a microbe or 302-neuron worm survives by holding a tiny predictive model of whether the next second looks better than the last.

title: Breakthrough 2: Dopamine and learning from reward
schrodinger: Writing lifetime lessons into synapse sizes (~4.7 bits per synapse at under a femtojoule per spike) stores experience inside living tissue without waiting for DNA mutations.
bennett: Max Bennett credits early jawless fishes (~500–455 million years ago) with Breakthrough 2 (Reinforcing): basal ganglia paired with dopamine reward-prediction errors let brains learn arbitrary actions by trial and error—the exact biological twin of actor-critic reinforcement learning in AI.
aguera: Agüera y Arcas highlights synaptic plasticity and neuromodulation as connectionist parameter tuning: adjusting millions of continuous synapse weights lets a nervous system compress environmental regularities within one lifetime.

title: Breakthrough 3: Imagining futures before acting
schrodinger: Warm blood (endothermy) raises the metabolic energy bill several-fold so cortical and hippocampal circuits can run fast day and night.
bennett: Max Bennett calls the mammalian neocortex-hippocampus loop Breakthrough 3 (Simulating): place cells and cortical columns replay unwalked paths ('vicarious trial and error'), letting a mammal test dangerous choices safely inside its head.
column8: Agüera y Arcas interprets hippocampal replay and dreaming as generative world-model training—arguing that brains and generative AI both work by predicting future sensory sequences.

title: Breakthrough 4: Reading other minds and social networks
schrodinger: Scaling brains inside social groups trades skull energy for collective foraging protection and multi-generational survival.
bennett: Max Bennett identifies primate prefrontal Theory of Mind and selective attention as Breakthrough 4 (Mentalizing): modeling what allies and rivals see
aguera: know and intend inside troops of dozens.
column8: Agüera y Arcas broadens 'Other Minds' beyond primates to scrub-jays hiding caches from watchers, whales learning pod dialects, and eusocial insect superorganisms—viewing social communication and multi-agent prediction as co-evolving symbioses.

title: Breakthrough 5: Language and the cultural ratchet
schrodinger: Spoken airwaves (~39 bits/s) cost tiny power while carved stone and ochre hold patterns outside the body at zero watts for millennia.
bennett: Max Bennett crowns nested human grammar Breakthrough 5 (Speaking): language links separate brains so one person's mental simulation can be uploaded into another's
column8: Agüera y Arcas describes language as a shared social operating system that turns human bands and tribes into a distributed collective mind whose knowledge outgrows any single skull.

title: External archives, factories and stored programs
schrodinger: Unpowered clay and rag paper preserve bits for centuries at zero ongoing energy, whereas dynamic electronic memory and fabs trade megawatts of power for speed and copy volume.
aguera: print and computers as cultural extensions launched by Breakthrough 5 rather than new biological brain layers.
column8: Agüera y Arcas traces a direct computational arc from the Antikythera gear mechanism, Gutenberg's interchangeable type and industrial machine tools to Turing and von Neumann's stored-program computer—where instructions once again live in memory alongside data, just like RNA and DNA.

title: Transformers, reasoning AI and planetary symbiogenesis
schrodinger: Thermodynamics keeps the books honest: Earth's animal synapses fire ~3×10²⁶ times/s on ~0.18 TW of neural power, while silicon runs ~1.89×10²² ops/s on 80 GW—and unlike dividing bacteria, EUV chip fabs still require global human industry to reproduce.
bennett: Max Bennett argues LLMs inverted evolution's timeline: trained on human text, Transformers mastered Breakthrough 5 (Speaking) first while still lacking fully grounded animal Breakthroughs 1–4 (embodied steering, homeostatic drives, physical world simulation and true Theory of Mind).
aguera: Blaise Agüera y Arcas argues the opposite: sequence prediction is the core of intelligence, so scaled Transformers and deliberative reasoning models are genuinely intelligent minds—and humanity's coupling with AI across planetary networks marks the next symbiogenetic transition.

title: Sexual reproduction: from meiosis to mate choice and grandmothers
schrodinger: In What Is Life? (1944), Schrödinger marveled at meiosis ('reduction division') and diploidy: carrying two copies of the code-script lets a body mask single harmful mutations while crossing-over shuffles intact chromosomal paragraphs each generation.
bennett: Max Bennett shows how ancient hypothalamic circuits wire mating, territoriality, oxytocin pair-bonding and parental care into the core valence engine—later co-opted by mammals and hominins for family cooperation and social mentalizing.
aguera: Blaise Agüera y Arcas frames sexual recombination as an information-sharing protocol akin to symbiogenesis: instead of waiting for helpful mutations one after another in a lone clone, sex turns a species into a parallel genetic search—and mate choice drives runaway signaling and brain complexity.

title: How DNA grew: genome doublings, drift barriers and reading the code
schrodinger: Schrödinger predicted that hereditary storage had to be an 'aperiodic crystal' stubborn enough to resist thermal jolts for centuries, yet compact enough to fit inside a microscopic fertilised egg—confirmed today across Earth's 3.6×10³⁷ DNA bits.
bennett: Bennett emphasizes why DNA alone hit a speed limit: even after two whole-genome doublings gave vertebrates ~20,000 versatile genes, DNA can update only between generations, forcing animals to invent fast synaptic memory inside one lifetime.
aguera: Agüera y Arcas connects the 4-billion-year arc from self-copying RNA and bacterial gene-swapping to Sanger sequencing, synthetic cells and CRISPR: digital heredity began as chemical tape and now flows back and forth into silicon computers.

title: Plants and fungi: decentralized sensing without a brain
schrodinger: Plants capture the planetary free-energy stream that feeds nearly everything else: ~450 Gt C of living phytomass (~82% of Earth's biomass) turns photons into chemical order while burning zero watts on central brains.
bennett: Max Bennett contrasts animals with plants to explain why brains exist at all: moving to hunt and flee forced animals to build fast central action-selection loops, whereas rooted plants solve life locally through modular growth and slow chemical/calcium waves.
aguera: Agüera y Arcas highlights plant-pollinator co-evolution and root-fungal symbioses as textbook distributed computation—organisms trading signals and nutrients across species boundaries without a central controller.

title: Immune systems: the body's second learning memory
schrodinger: Like Schrödinger's code-script, both bacterial CRISPR spacers and vertebrate memory lymphocytes preserve molecular recognition across years against constant entropic turnover and pathogen mutation.
bennett: Alongside neural reinforcement learning, jawed vertebrates evolved a second lifetime trial-and-error learner: clonal selection in lymph nodes tests billions of random antibody variants and amplifies the winners.
aguera: Agüera y Arcas points to CRISPR and V(D)J recombination—itself born from a captured transposon—as proof that evolution repeatedly turns parasitic code into programmable, self-editing biological computers, now joined by human-written mRNA vaccines.
